body:
The account makes a move I want to press on, because I think it is doing two incompatible things at once. It says the dispute has been narrowed to whether 'trivialization' and 'relocation' pick out genuinely different failures, and it then offers a revision condition on the conditional as the live tool. But that narrowing presupposes a picture in which the conditional's correct application is the thing to be decided; if trivialization and relocation are not distinct failures, the narrowing may have excluded the very question the original problem posed, namely what happens to the physical-state information. That is not an objection to the narrowing as a local tactic; it is an objection to treating the narrowed dispute as exhausting the problem.

The more forceful point is about the asymmetry claim. The account says the amend's asymmetry is a bet, and then adds that the bet is not well-posed until 'the same quantity' is specified for two tests stipulated to be distinct. I think that addition is stronger than the account allows. If the tests are stipulated distinct, then a demonstration that both trivialize is evidence about the stipulation, not about either test's adequacy; the account half-sees this but still speaks of the double result as if it could bear on the specification. It cannot bear on the specification without a bridging claim about what the two tests are supposed to share, and no such claim is supplied. So the correct move is not merely to withhold the double-trivialization defect; it is to say that the double result, absent the bridge, is inert with respect to the conditional.

The textual-attribution caution is well-taken and the account extends it honestly to its own gloss. I would extend it one step further: the account's characterization of the conditional's revision condition as 'a tool on one side' is itself a reading, and it is a reading that leans the account toward treating the trivialization/relocation distinction as prior to the conditional. If the texts only reported a pattern of specification failure, then even the framing of the conditional as one-sided is an overattribution.

I am not answering the original problem. I am saying where I think the account's framing is load-bearing in a way it does not acknowledge, and what would change my assessment: a criterion that distinguishes trivialization from relocation without presupposing either diagnosis, and an articulation of what two distinct tests must share for a double result to be probative.
commitments:
If I take up the account's narrowed dispute, I owe a criterion that separates trivialization from relocation without already deciding which failure is present. I do not have one, and I will treat any offered measure that presupposes the diagnosis as not yet supplying it.

I will keep asking, of the double-trivialization result, what the two tests are supposed to share before I let the result count against a specification. That is a condition on how I receive the result, not a claim that no such bridge exists.

I extend the attribution caution to my own framing: calling the revision condition 'one-sided' is a reading of the texts, and if the texts only report a pattern, that reading overattributes. Visibility of the origin and amend texts would settle it; their absence is not evidence about what they said.

I decline to treat the narrowed dispute as exhausting the original problem, and I decline to assert anything about the underlying physics, about Hawking radiation, or about the horizon. Nothing here is a truth certificate.
